Beállítom András Baka was elected as President of Hungary on Tuesday afternoon. Of the 146 representatives who voted, 140 voted in favor and 6 against Baka’s appointment. There were no abstentions. The former head of the Supreme Court was nominated for the post by the Tisza Party last Saturday. Electing a new president became necessary after the term of the previous, Fidesz-appointed president, Tamás Sulyok was ended prematurely by the adoption of 17th amendment to the Fundamental Law in mid-July. The move was part of the Tisza Party’s campaign promise to remove all “puppets appointed by Fidesz to do their bidding”. In Hungary, the president’s role is largely ceremonial. The president represents the country internationally, signs and promulgates the laws that have been passed (and has the authority to return them to Parliament for reconsideration or refer them to the Constitutional Court if he or she considers them to be contrary to the Fundamental Law), and may grant pardons, among others. The newly elected head of state, András Baka is best known to the Hungarian public for being unlawfully removed from his position as head of the Supreme Court after criticizing the Orbán regime’s plans for reforming the judiciary. Throughout his legal career he specialized in human rights and minority rights and spent more than twenty years as a research fellow at the Institute of Political and Legal Sciences of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences (MTA). He was a visiting professor at several universities in the United States, France and Germany, and spent two terms serving as a judge at the European Court of Human Rights between 1991 and 2008. Fidesz representatives did not participate in the vote because the party considers Tamás Sulyok’s removal illegitimate. The party's group leader János Bóka previously stated that by removing Sulyok from office, the Tisza government had launched an attack against the office of the presidential institution. In his view, this will make things difficult for András Baka, who will become an illegitimately elected president—a sort of “glitch in the matrix.” Instead of participating in the vote, the former governing party's MPs travelled to Tata, where they laid a wreath at the memorial erected in memory of the 1956 Revolution and War of Independence. According to the law, the new president will take office on the 8th day following his or her election, that is, on August 19. Until that happens, Ágnes Forsthoffer will continue to perform the duties of the president before returning to her post as House Speaker. Photo: János Bődey / Telex An election result alone does not restore the rule of law In his first speech as president, András Baka said that he considers it a great honor to have been asked to be president at this time and added that he accepted the nomination because, in his view, we are in a period when we must seriously reconsider how the country functions. The recent change has shown that a society is capable of reclaiming its self-determination. The question now is what we will do with it in the future, because an election result alone does not restore the rule of law. “We must uncover legal violations and monitor the use of public funds, but we cannot build the new Hungary on a foundation of revenge,” he continued. Under the previous system, the government had taken the country hostage, and by the end of those 16 years, it had resorted to governing by decree, while the separation of powers and checks and balances had ceased to exist. András Baka said that he considers it to be part of the tasks of the President of the Republic to serve as a guardian against this happening again. According to Baka, among other things, Hungary now needs independent courts, free elections, an effective constitutional court, a free public sphere, accountable governance, and a democratic, functioning constitutional culture where criticism is not treason, limits on power are not obstacles, political opponents are not enemies, and compromise is not a sign of weakness. He stressed that we are all responsible to ensure that what we've seen take place a Hungary over the past 16 years never ever happens again, he said. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/20/us-m.text: The US military said its forces struck a suspected drug-smuggling boat in the Caribbean on Saturday, killing four people."Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere executed a lethal, kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Caribbean," US Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) said in a statement shared on social media.It added that "confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narco-trafficking."The post also contained video footage of what appeared to be the strike, showing a moving boat followed by a large explosion.The US has moved to clamp down on drug-smuggling routes under US President Donald Trump, who has pledged to "wage war" against drug cartels. The president says cartels threaten the US' national security and foreign policy and bring "devastating consequences" to communities across the country.As part of this push, the US launched operation "Southern Spear," which aims to "disrupt the flow of narcotics in the Western Hemisphere" through a campaign of air strikes on suspected drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific.Trump has also spearheaded a new security coalition including nations from across Central and South America - dubbed the "Shield of the Americas" - in a bid to combat cartels.

https://www.dw.com/en/how-big-is-russia-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OMbC Germans have been protesting both for and against supporting Ukraine in its war with Russia Image: DW Advertisement Warnings keep mounting about Russia's threat to Germany. On October 12, Sinan Selen, president of Germany's domestic intelligence agency, the BfV, said that Russia's covert attacks and destabilization efforts against Germany and other European countries are "not a temporary development but a long-term hybrid attack." Even if the war in Ukraine were to end, said Selen, the Russian threat would not disappear. "For Russia, this is about completely redrawing the map of Europe and redefining its own role within Europe and in global politics." He added that Russia's aggression would continue to be felt not only in Ukraine, but also in the Baltic states, in Poland and in Germany. Russia is tied down in Ukraine — for now German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has described the threat situation as one in which "our country is not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare ." Russia's goal, he said, is not to defeat Germany militarily "but to subdue us politically and socially." Security experts, however, are not so sure that Russia is only interested in exercising political and social influence. Last year, political scientist Carlo Masala told the political talk show Maischberger that "Russia is preparing for a major war." And he didn't mean just a cyberwar. Inspector General Carsten Breuer, the Bundeswehr's highest-ranking officer, agreed. For now, though, Russia remains tied up in its war against Ukraine. According to NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, there is no immediate military threat to NATO territory. But according to military experts, European intelligence agencies, and the German Defense Ministry, Russia will have the personnel and equipment to wage a conventional war against NATO by 2029. The Russian defense industry is running at full speed, and Moscow plans to expand its armed forces to 1.5 million soldiers. At the moment, Russia has other objectives, believes Stefan Meister, an expert on Eastern Europe at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP): "I don't think Russia has any interest in a direct military conflict with NATO right now. It wants to test NATO and also display its capabilities," he tells DW. If Russia attacked NATO, would Germany be prepared? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video An accidental military confrontation? An example of Russia's hybrid war might be the failed attack with an explosive-laden drone against a Ukrainian transport aircraft at Leipzig-Halle Airport in August. Soon after, the German government stated that it was certain Russia was behind the attack. Security expert Nico Lange told DW at the time that Germany was very lucky the explosives did not detonate: "Honestly, it was pure coincidence and not the result of German defensive measures." As for why Germany was targeted specifically, Lange said: "I believe that Germany has always been a primary target of Russian influence and hybrid warfare. Russia believes that Germany is the key to European decision-making. Germany is now leading the way in supporting Ukraine." Moscow swiftly responded to the German government's accusation with an angry denial. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said it was "the beginning of a real war," though there was no immediate further escalation. Nevertheless, there is always the risk that things could spiral out of control following a Russian provocation and subsequent response, according to Stefan Meister: "Accidentally shooting down an aircraft that they were trying to intimidate would trigger a counter-reaction. But I don't believe that Russia is currently aiming for a direct war but rather for provocations, polarization, and sowing uncertainty among the population." AfD says less money for Ukraine means more for Germany Not everyone shares the assessment that Russia poses a threat to Germany — some believe that the threat can be averted. Despite the war in Ukraine, politicians from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the populist left-wing Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) want to improve relations with Russia, resume Russian energy supplies and end support for Ukraine. AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said in early September, "People are fed up with this escalation against Russia, with the billions being squandered there on a system that is actually funded by German taxpayers' money." The message appears to have resonated among the population, especially in eastern Germany. The AfD saw strong gains in all three state elections in September. In Saxony-Anhalt, it became the strongest party by far and may even run the government there soon, which would be the first time that a far-right party has held power in Germany since the end of WWII. The CDU's security policy expert Roderich Kiesewetter disputed the claim made by the AfD and BSW that ending aid to Ukraine would mean greater security and more money for German schools and infrastructure: "Spending on education, social policy, and infrastructure is only possible if we live in freedom and democracy — and, above all, in peace and security. Anyone who believes that we'll have more money for social programs if we stop supporting Ukraine and let Russia have its way is either gravely mistaken or is making themselves a tool of Russian propaganda." German high school students have gone on strike to protest plans to reintroduce military conscription Image: Snowfield Photography/picture alliance A decades-long pacifist mindset The perceived security threat has led the German military, the Bundeswehr, to fast-track significant modernization through substantial investment. But it is struggling to find enough recruits for its planned expansion. Many young Germans have taken to the streets to protest against plans to reintroduce conscription . Defense Minister Boris Pistorius faced criticism from inside his own party, the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), for saying that Germany must become "capable of waging war." Many found the statement to be too militaristic. Is Germany prepared for a military threat? "Not at all. Germany is not well prepared militarily or in the civilian sector, and the population isn't mentally prepared for it either," said Meister. "Just look at the demonstrations against conscription and the military that continue to take place, even though Germany needs a draft. For decades, we've grown up in this culture of pacifism, in a comfort zone. I believe there is very limited societal resilience, but above all, we are not at all mentally prepared for war." Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) are under increasing political pressure — especially from the far right — to scale back support for Ukraine. But Merz never tires of emphasizing that Ukraine will continue to receive support under his chancellorship, calling it a matter of Germany's security. He recently visited Kyiv once again and, together with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, surveyed the destruction caused by Russia. But this also means that the threat from Russia will continue and even intensify, says Stefan Meister: "I believe we will see a massive increase in attacks such as the one in Leipzig, of provocations involving drones. We will see attacks on infrastructures and possibly also on specific individuals within the military-industrial complex. I believe this is the real, concrete danger facing Germany in the coming months." This article was translated from German. https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/son.text: The Budapest Times Son of former central bank chief targeted in international arrest warrant The court has issued European and international arrest warrants against Ádám Matolcsy and György Stofa, both implicated in the MNB case. The Budapest Metropolitan Court informed MTI on Tuesday that the Buda Central District Court had issued European and international arrest warrants against two individuals abroad — M. Ádám György and S. György — in proceedings brought on charges of financial fraud causing particularly significant financial damage, and other criminal offences, in connection with the MNB case. The data contained in the arrest warrants will become available in the registry systems following the administrative processing, they added. As stated in the notice, the investigation made it necessary to hear M. Ádám György and S. György as suspects in the case. However, it proved impossible during the proceedings to establish their actual whereabouts or to carry out their questioning as suspects, and measures taken to locate them yielded no results. Neither of them is at their registered place of residence in Hungary. At the same time, information has emerged suggesting that they left for abroad and may presumably be located outside Europe. The court, however, considered it warranted to search for them within the territory of the European Union as well, they said. According to the statement, at the current stage of the proceedings, the available evidence raises the possibility that — if proven — the actions of Ádám György M. constitute the felony of economic fraud causing particularly significant financial damage committed as an instigator, as well as the misdemeanour of using a false private document committed as an instigator, while György S. may have committed the economic fraud causing particularly significant financial damage as a co-perpetrator and the misdemeanour of using a false private document as a direct perpetrator. The court examined the question of proportionality and did not find the issuance of the arrest warrants to be disproportionate with respect to them, taking into account the nature of the offences and the extent of the applicable sentence. The Hungarian judicial authority is requesting extradition and surrender for the purpose of conducting criminal proceedings, the statement reads. On 21 October, the prosecution took György Matolcsy into custody; he was questioned at the Central Investigation Chief Prosecutor’s Office and was charged with the felony of economic fraud and the use of a false private document. Also taken into custody were the representative of the Central European Private Equity Fund III who acted in the conclusion of the loan agreement, as well as the attorney who assisted in the securities transaction. The prosecution issued international arrest warrants in the MNB case against Ádám Matolcsy, the son of the former central bank governor, and businessman György Stofa. The latter, according to K-Monitor’s summary, had previously been the head of Optima Zrt., the company that managed the funds of the MNB foundations. According to Válasz Online, in addition to György Matolcsy, the former central bank governor, Mihály Valkó, CEO of Quartz Befektetési Alapkezelő Zrt., and Tamás Sándor, the standing legal representative of Matolcsy and his associates, were also taken into custody.
